To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Jr(a+W) and Jr(a–) phenotypes result from expression of the Jr(a) antigen on the surface of RBCs.

the JR blood group is determined by the ABCG2 gene, that the JRa antigen is expressed in the presence of a normal ABCG2 allele and that the JRb antigen is expressed only when the JRa allele is present.
the JR blood group is a complex system in which the expression of JR antigens can vary depending on the genetic background of the RBCs.
In summary, our research is concerned with

(i) identification of the Jr(a+) phenotype, (ii) identification of the Jra+ phenotype, (iii) identification of the JR+ phenotype, (iv) identification of the null phenotype, (v) determination of the Jr(a+W/+) phenotype, (vi) identification of the Sr(a+) phenotype, and (vii) determination of the Jra–/Sr(a+) phenotype.
the identification of alleles of the ABCG2 gene that alter the expression of JR antigens.

the identification of Jr(a)‐negative RBCs that are nonreactive or weakly reactive with polyclonal or monoclonal anti–JRα, and with the identification of the underlying molecular basis for the expression or lack of expression of JRα.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Jr(a+) RBCs are Jr(a+) and Jr(a–) RBCs are JR‐null.
Jr(a+W/+) and Jr(a+/+) RBCs express the JRa antigen, Jr(aW/+) and Jr(+W/+) RBCs do not, and Jr(a–) RBCs are nonreactive.
Jr(a+) is the most common allele, and Jr(a–) and Jr(a+W) are less common.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Jr(a–) and Jr(a+W/+) RBCs have a single allele (Jra) that encodes a protein with a single amino acid difference (R482W) compared with RBCs from Jr(a+W/−) donors.
Jr(a+W) is Jr(a+) and Jr(a–) is Jr(a–).
the Jr(a+) phenotype is associated with a normal expression of JR antigens and the Jr(aW) phenotype is associated with the expression of a weakly reactive form of the JR antigens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Jr(a+) phenotype can be caused by the presence of an ABCG2 null allele, but the Jr(a+) expression is not necessarily associated with the presence of an active gene product.
the expression of JR antigens is highly dependent upon the ABCG2 allele.
the Jr(a+) phenotype can be expressed in RBCs from homozygous Jr(a–) individuals.
